content: This review is an update of a previous Cochrane review from June 2012, which examined the use of cromolyn sodium for preventing chronic lung disease (CLD) in preterm infants. The 2016 update did not identify any new studies beyond the two included in the original review. CLD is a common condition in preterm infants, with a complex etiology that includes inflammation. Cromolyn sodium, a mast cell stabilizer, inhibits neutrophil activation and chemotaxis, which suggests it might play a role in preventing CLD. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether prophylactic administration of cromolyn sodium reduces the incidence of CLD at 28 days or 36 weeks' postmenstrual age (PMA), mortality, or the combined outcome of mortality and CLD at these time points in preterm infants. The search strategy followed Cochrane Neonatal's standard methods, including searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL up to May 12, 2016. Additional sources such as clinical trial databases, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving preterm infants, with cromolyn sodium administered within the first two weeks of life via nebulizer or metered-dose inhaler (with or without a spacer). Eligible studies needed to report at least one of the following outcomes: overall mortality, CLD at 28 days, CLD at 36 weeks' PMA, or the combined outcome of mortality and CLD at 28 days. Data collection and analysis adhered to Cochrane's standard methods. Risk ratios (RR) and risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, while mean differences (MD) with 95% CI were used for continuous data. A fixed-effect model was employed for meta-analysis, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. The quality of evidence for key outcomes was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The review identified two eligible studies, which included a total of 64 infants. Prophylactic use of cromolyn sodium did not result in a statistically significant reduction in the combined outcome of mortality and CLD at 28 days (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.52; RD 0.03, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.27; I² = 0%). Similarly, there was no significant effect on mortality at 28 days (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.52 to 3.29; RD 0.06, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.26; I² = 73% and 87%, respectively) or on CLD at 28 days (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.64; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.20; I² = 40% and 38%, respectively). At 36 weeks' PMA, there was also no significant effect on CLD (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.63; RD 0.08, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.44; based on one trial with 26 infants). Among survivors, there was no significant difference in CLD at 28 days (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.63; RD -0.02, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.26; I² = 0%) or at 36 weeks' PMA (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.38 to 2.87; RD 0.02, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.43; based on one trial with 22 infants). Cromolyn sodium prophylaxis did not significantly affect other outcomes, including overall neonatal mortality, air leaks, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, sepsis, or duration of mechanical ventilation. No adverse effects were reported. The quality of evidence was rated as very low for mortality at 28 days and low for all other outcomes. The evidence was downgraded due to study design issues (risk of bias in one study), inconsistency between the two studies (high I² values for mortality at 28 days), and imprecision (small sample sizes). Given these limitations, further research on this topic does not appear to be justified. In conclusion, there is no evidence from randomized trials to support the use of cromolyn sodium for preventing CLD in preterm infants. Therefore, cromolyn sodium cannot be recommended for this purpose.
